concepts.def: The synthesis of RNA using one strand of the DNA of a gene as a template. RNA polymerase moves along the template strand, and free RNA nucleotides that pair with the exposed DNA bases are linked together into a single strand of RNA whose base sequence is complementary to the template. Only the region of DNA making up the gene is transcribed, not the whole molecule, and the DNA is left unchanged.

The enzyme that carries out transcription. It binds to the DNA at the start of a gene, separates the two strands of the double helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds between them, moves along the template strand and forms covalent bonds between the sugar of one RNA nucleotide and the phosphate of the next, so building the RNA strand. Unlike DNA replication, transcription needs no helicase and no primer: RNA polymerase both opens the DNA and starts the new strand.

The one strand of a gene that is transcribed. RNA nucleotides are positioned by complementary base pairing with the bases of this strand, so the RNA is complementary to the template strand and has the same base sequence as the other (non-template) strand of the gene, except that uracil takes the place of thymine.

The pairing of each free RNA nucleotide with the DNA base opposite it on the template strand: cytosine with guanine, guanine with cytosine, thymine on the DNA with adenine on the RNA, and adenine on the DNA template strand with uracil on the RNA strand. The pairs are held by hydrogen bonds, which are weak enough to break again so that the completed RNA separates from the template and the two DNA strands re-pair.

The base found in RNA in place of the thymine of DNA. Uracil pairs with adenine, so wherever the DNA template strand has adenine, the RNA strand transcribed from it has uracil. RNA never contains thymine.

The property that a single strand of DNA can be used as a template for transcription, repeatedly, without its base sequence changing. The template strand is read by pairing, not consumed or rewritten; after the RNA is released the hydrogen bonds between the two DNA strands re-form and the gene is exactly as it was. Because of this, the same base sequence can be transcribed throughout the life of a cell.

A body cell (not a gamete) that has stopped dividing, such as a neuron or a cardiac muscle cell. Such a cell never replicates its DNA again, so the DNA it contains must serve as the template for all its transcription for the rest of its life, which in humans can be many decades. Its base sequences must therefore be conserved throughout the life of the cell.

The process by which the information in a gene is used to produce a functional product, for a protein-coding gene by transcription of the gene into mRNA followed by translation into a polypeptide. Not all genes in a cell are expressed at any given time: each cell type transcribes only some of its genes. Because transcription is the first stage of expression, it is a key stage at which the expression of a gene can be switched on or off.

The synthesis of a polypeptide on a ribosome, in which the base sequence of an mRNA molecule determines the sequence of amino acids. The mRNA is read in groups of three bases (codons), each specifying one amino acid, and the amino acids, brought by tRNA, are joined by peptide bonds in the order the codons dictate. Translation takes place on ribosomes in the cytoplasm (free or on rough endoplasmic reticulum), not in the nucleus.

A chain of amino acids linked by peptide bonds, produced by translation. Its amino acid sequence is determined by the base sequence of the mRNA it was translated from, and ultimately by the base sequence of the gene. A protein consists of one or more polypeptides, often modified after translation.

The RNA molecule transcribed from a protein-coding gene that carries the gene's base sequence, as a series of codons, to a ribosome. During translation the mRNA binds to the small subunit of the ribosome, which moves along it so that each codon in turn is presented for pairing with a tRNA anticodon.

The structure on which translation occurs, made of a small subunit and a large subunit, each consisting of rRNA and protein. The mRNA binds to the small subunit. The large subunit has binding sites for tRNA, and two tRNAs can bind simultaneously, so that the amino acid carried by one can be joined by a peptide bond to the polypeptide held by the other. The ribosome catalyses peptide bond formation and moves along the mRNA one codon at a time.

A small RNA molecule that carries a specific amino acid to the ribosome. Each tRNA has an anticodon of three bases at one end and its amino acid attached at the other end; the amino acid is attached before the tRNA reaches the ribosome, so the tRNA whose anticodon pairs with the codon delivers the amino acid that codon specifies. After its amino acid has been joined to the polypeptide the tRNA leaves the ribosome and can be reloaded and used again.

A sequence of three bases on an mRNA molecule that specifies one amino acid, or signals the start or stop of translation. The codons of an mRNA are read one after another, without overlap, in a fixed reading frame set by the start codon.

The sequence of three bases on a tRNA molecule that is complementary to a codon on mRNA. During translation the anticodon pairs with the codon by complementary base pairing (A with U, C with G), held by hydrogen bonds, so that only the tRNA carrying the amino acid the codon specifies can bind. The anticodon is complementary to the codon, not identical to it: the codon AUG pairs with the anticodon UAC.

The feature of the genetic code that each amino acid is specified by a codon of three bases. Three bases are the minimum needed: with four bases, codons of two bases give only 4 × 4 = 16 combinations, too few for the 20 amino acids used in polypeptides, whereas codons of three bases give 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 combinations, more than enough.

The feature of the genetic code that most amino acids are specified by more than one codon: 61 of the 64 codons code for only 20 amino acids, so for example the four codons GGU, GGC, GGA and GGG all code for glycine. The code is degenerate but not ambiguous: each codon specifies only one amino acid. One consequence is that some base substitutions do not change the amino acid sequence of the polypeptide.

The feature of the genetic code that, with only minor exceptions, the same codons specify the same amino acids in all living organisms. This is evidence that all organisms share a common ancestry, and it means that a gene transferred from one species to another is translated into the same polypeptide, which is what makes the production of human proteins by genetically modified bacteria possible.

A table listing all 64 mRNA codons and the amino acid, or start or stop signal, that each specifies. To deduce the amino acid sequence coded by an mRNA, the base sequence is divided into successive codons of three bases starting from the start codon, and each codon is looked up in the table. The table is written for mRNA codons, so a DNA template sequence must first be converted to its complementary mRNA sequence before the table can be used.

AUG is the start codon: it marks where translation begins and it also codes for the amino acid methionine, so the first amino acid of a newly made polypeptide is methionine. UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons: they code for no amino acid, and when the ribosome reaches one, translation ends and the polypeptide is released. Any bases after a stop codon are not translated.

The stage of translation in which the polypeptide chain is lengthened. With two tRNAs bound to the ribosome, a peptide bond forms between the amino acid carried by the newly arrived tRNA and the growing polypeptide, so that the chain is transferred to the new tRNA. The ribosome then moves along the mRNA by exactly one codon, the tRNA that has given up the chain leaves, and the next codon is exposed for the next tRNA to bind. The cycle repeats one amino acid at a time.

The covalent bond that links amino acids in a polypeptide, formed by a condensation reaction between the carboxyl group of the last amino acid in the chain and the amino group of the next amino acid. It is formed on the ribosome during elongation and is not a hydrogen bond; the hydrogen bonds involved in translation are those between codon and anticodon.

A mutation that alters a single base pair in the DNA of a gene: a base substitution, in which one base is replaced by another, or the insertion or deletion of a single base. A substitution changes one codon of the mRNA and so may change one amino acid of the polypeptide, or may have no effect if the new codon specifies the same amino acid. Mutations occur in the DNA, and the change reaches the protein through transcription and translation.

concepts.term: Sickle cell mutation (an example of a point mutation affecting protein structure)
concepts.def: A base substitution in the gene for the beta chain of haemoglobin that changes the sixth codon of the mRNA from GAG to GUG, so that valine is inserted in place of glutamic acid at one position in the polypeptide. Although only one amino acid out of 146 is changed, the altered haemoglobin molecules stick together and form fibres when the oxygen concentration is low, distorting red blood cells into a sickle shape and causing sickle cell anaemia.

The consequence of inserting or deleting a number of bases that is not a multiple of three within the coding sequence of a gene. Because codons are read consecutively in groups of three from the start codon, the insertion or deletion of a single base shifts the reading frame, so that every codon after the mutation is read differently and the amino acid sequence from that point onward is changed, usually producing a non-functional protein.

The two chemically different ends of a strand of DNA or RNA. The 5' end has a phosphate group attached to carbon 5 of the terminal sugar; the 3' end has a hydroxyl group on carbon 3 of the terminal sugar. The two strands of a DNA double helix are antiparallel, so the 5' end of one strand lies opposite the 3' end of the other. Base sequences are written 5' to 3' unless stated otherwise.

Transcription is 5' to 3' because RNA polymerase can only add a nucleotide to the free 3' hydroxyl group of the growing RNA strand, so the RNA is synthesized from its 5' end towards its 3' end, and the antiparallel DNA template strand is therefore read 3' to 5'. Translation is 5' to 3' because the ribosome moves along the mRNA from the 5' end towards the 3' end, so the codon nearest the 5' end is translated first and the polypeptide is built from its amino terminus to its carboxyl terminus.

A non-coding sequence of DNA adjacent to the start of a gene, to which RNA polymerase and transcription factors bind so that transcription can be initiated. The promoter positions RNA polymerase at the start of the gene, determining which strand is used as the template and where transcription begins; it is not itself part of the sequence that codes for the polypeptide.

A protein that binds to the promoter (or to another regulatory sequence) of a gene and is required in eukaryotes for RNA polymerase to bind to the promoter and begin transcription. Different cell types contain different transcription factors, so the same gene can be transcribed in one cell type and not in another even though the DNA is identical. This is an example of how transcription is initiated at the promoter; students are not required to name particular transcription factors.

DNA sequences that do not code for polypeptides. Most eukaryotic DNA is non-coding, but much of it has a function. Examples are sequences that regulate gene expression, such as promoters and enhancers, to which proteins bind; introns within genes; telomeres at the ends of chromosomes; and the genes for rRNA and tRNA, which are transcribed into RNA molecules that function without ever being translated.

A region of repetitive non-coding DNA at each end of a eukaryotic chromosome. Telomeres do not code for polypeptides; they protect the ends of the chromosome so that the coding sequences near the ends are not lost or damaged.

An intron is a non-coding sequence within a eukaryotic gene that is transcribed into the pre-mRNA but is then removed, so it does not appear in the mature mRNA and is not translated. An exon is a sequence of the gene that is retained in the mature mRNA after splicing. The gene itself is not altered by splicing: introns are cut out of the RNA transcript, not out of the DNA.

The changes made to the initial RNA transcript (pre-mRNA) of a eukaryotic gene in the nucleus to produce mature mRNA: the introns are removed and the exons are spliced together, a 5' cap is added to the 5' end and a poly-A tail is added to the 3' end. Only the mature mRNA leaves the nucleus and is translated.

Modifications added to the two ends of a eukaryotic mRNA transcript: a modified guanine nucleotide (the cap) added to the 5' end, and a chain of many adenine nucleotides (the poly-A tail) added to the 3' end. They stabilize the mRNA transcript, protecting it from being broken down, so that it survives to be translated. They are not translated and add no amino acids to the polypeptide.

The splicing together of different combinations of the exons of one pre-mRNA to produce different mature mRNAs, which are translated into different polypeptides. Because of alternative splicing a single gene can code for several variants of a protein, and the number of different polypeptides an organism produces is far greater than its number of genes. The base sequence of the gene is not changed.

The sequence of events that assembles a ribosome on an mRNA. The small ribosomal subunit binds to the 5' end of the mRNA and moves along it until it reaches the start codon AUG. The initiator tRNA, carrying methionine and with an anticodon complementary to AUG, binds to the start codon. The large subunit then attaches, with the initiator tRNA in the P site, and a second tRNA can bind to the next codon in the A site so that elongation can begin.

The three tRNA binding sites of the ribosome. During elongation a tRNA carrying the next amino acid enters the A site, where its anticodon pairs with the codon; the tRNA holding the growing polypeptide occupies the P site; a peptide bond forms so that the polypeptide is transferred onto the amino acid in the A site; the ribosome then moves one codon along the mRNA, so the tRNA now carrying the polypeptide moves to the P site, the tRNA that has given up the chain moves to the E site and exits, and the A site is free for the next tRNA.

Changes made to a polypeptide after translation that are needed before it can function. Examples are the removal of sections of the chain, the formation of disulfide bonds between cysteines, the addition of carbohydrate groups and the assembly of several polypeptides into one protein. Many polypeptides are not functional as they leave the ribosome.

The two-stage modification by which insulin is made from a single polypeptide. Translation produces pre-proinsulin; in the first stage its signal sequence (a short section at the amino terminus that directs it into the endoplasmic reticulum) is removed, giving proinsulin, which folds and forms disulfide bonds. In the second stage a central section of proinsulin (the C-peptide) is cut out, leaving the two remaining sections, the A and B chains, held together by the disulfide bonds. This is functional insulin, 51 amino acids in two chains, although it was coded for by one gene and translated as one polypeptide.

A large protein complex in the cytoplasm and nucleus that breaks down proteins that are damaged or no longer needed into their amino acids. The amino acids are recycled and used in the synthesis of new proteins. Protein breakdown by proteasomes is a normal, continuous activity of a healthy cell; it is not something that happens only when proteins are damaged or when the cell is starved.

All the proteins present in a cell (or organism) at a particular time. The proteome changes as conditions change, and sustaining a functional proteome requires constant protein breakdown and synthesis: proteins that are no longer required are broken down by proteasomes while the proteins the cell currently needs are translated, using amino acids from the pool that breakdown replenishes.

mcqs.q: Which statement describes the roles of RNA polymerase in transcription?
options: It separates the DNA strands and links RNA nucleotides, positioned by pairing with the template strand, into one RNA strand.
It links RNA nucleotides into a strand once helicase has opened the DNA and a primer has been laid down.
It copies both DNA strands of the gene at the same time, producing a double-stranded RNA molecule from the gene.
It joins amino acids together, one after another, in the order specified by the base sequence of the gene.
mcqs.specStatementText: Transcription: RNA polymerase makes an RNA copy of one gene
mcqs.explain: RNA polymerase binds to the gene, separates the DNA strands, positions free RNA nucleotides by complementary base pairing with the template strand and forms the covalent bonds that join them into a single RNA strand.
rationales: RNA polymerase binds to the gene, separates the DNA strands, positions free RNA nucleotides by complementary base pairing with the template strand and forms the covalent bonds that join them into a single RNA strand.

A student who transfers the replication machinery to transcription picks this. RNA polymerase separates the DNA strands itself and needs no primer; helicase and primase are not involved in transcription.
A student who models transcription on replication picks this. Only one strand, the template strand, is transcribed, and the product is a single strand of RNA.
A student who has swapped transcription and translation picks this. Amino acids are joined during translation on a ribosome; RNA polymerase joins RNA nucleotides, not amino acids.

mcqs.q: A section of the DNA template strand of a gene has the base sequence TACGCAT. What is the base sequence of the RNA transcribed from this section?
options: UACGCAU
AUGCGUA
UAGCGAU
ATGCGTA
mcqs.specStatementText: Base pairing sets the RNA sequence; hydrogen bonds let it go
mcqs.explain: Each RNA base is complementary to the template base opposite it: T pairs with A, A on the template pairs with U, C with G and G with C, giving AUGCGUA.
rationales: A student who copies the template like-for-like, only swapping T for U, picks this. The RNA is complementary to the template strand, not identical to it.
Each RNA base is complementary to the template base opposite it: T pairs with A, A on the template pairs with U, C with G and G with C, giving AUGCGUA.
A student who places uracil opposite thymine, and adenine opposite adenine, picks this. Uracil pairs with adenine on the template; thymine on the template pairs with adenine on the RNA.
A student who applies the DNA pairing rules and writes T opposite A picks this. RNA contains uracil, not thymine, so adenine on the template strand pairs with uracil on the RNA.

mcqs.q: During transcription, what holds each RNA nucleotide in position against the DNA template strand while it is being added to the growing RNA?
options: Covalent bonds made by RNA polymerase between the RNA base and the DNA base opposite it.
Hydrogen bonds between identical bases, so the RNA is an exact copy of the template.
Hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, which break again when the RNA is released.
Hydrogen bonds between adenine and thymine, since RNA contains the same four bases as DNA.
mcqs.specStatementText: Base pairing sets the RNA sequence; hydrogen bonds let it go
mcqs.explain: Complementary base pairing between the RNA nucleotide and the template base is held by hydrogen bonds. These are weak and temporary, so the completed RNA separates from the DNA and the DNA strands re-pair.
rationales: A student who thinks the enzyme bonds the RNA to the DNA picks this. RNA polymerase forms covalent bonds between successive RNA nucleotides along the backbone; base pairs are held by hydrogen bonds.
A student who expects a like-for-like copy picks this. Bases pair with their complements (A with U, C with G), so the RNA is complementary to the template, not identical to it.

Complementary base pairing between the RNA nucleotide and the template base is held by hydrogen bonds. These are weak and temporary, so the completed RNA separates from the DNA and the DNA strands re-pair.
A student who forgets that RNA contains uracil picks this. Adenine on the DNA template strand pairs with uracil on the RNA strand; there is no thymine in RNA.

mcqs.q: A neuron formed before birth does not divide again, yet it transcribes the same genes throughout a lifetime of many decades. Which statement explains how this is possible?
options: Each round of transcription slightly alters the template, so the neuron periodically replicates its DNA to restore the gene.
Because the neuron does not replicate its DNA again, its base sequences need not be conserved and can change freely.
Transcription copies both strands of the gene just as replication does, so every round of transcription renews the gene.
Transcription reads the template strand without altering its base sequence, so the sequence is conserved for life.
mcqs.specStatementText: A DNA template can be read again and again without changing
mcqs.explain: A single DNA strand can be used as a template for transcription without its base sequence changing. In a somatic cell that does not divide, the sequences are conserved and reused for the life of the cell.
rationales: A student who thinks a template wears out picks this. The template is read by base pairing and left unchanged, and a non-dividing neuron does not replicate its DNA at all.
A student who thinks DNA matters only when copied picks this. The neuron's DNA is the template for all its transcription, so a changed sequence would change every transcript for the rest of its life.

A student who models transcription on replication picks this. Only the template strand is transcribed, into single-stranded RNA; the gene persists because transcription does not change it, not because it is re-copied.

A single DNA strand can be used as a template for transcription without its base sequence changing. In a somatic cell that does not divide, the sequences are conserved and reused for the life of the cell.

mcqs.q: Developing red blood cells produce large amounts of the beta chain of haemoglobin, but liver cells produce none, although both cell types contain the gene. Which statement explains the difference?
options: The gene is transcribed in developing red blood cells but not in liver cells, so liver cells make no mRNA for the protein.
Liver cells lost the gene when they differentiated, so they no longer contain the DNA sequence for the beta chain.
Both cell types transcribe the gene, but only red blood cells translate the mRNA into the beta chain polypeptide.
Both cell types make the beta chain, but liver cells break the protein down as soon as it has been produced.
mcqs.specStatementText: Transcription is where gene expression is switched on or off
mcqs.explain: Not all genes in a cell are expressed at any given time. Transcription is the first stage of gene expression, so a gene that is not transcribed in a cell type gives no mRNA and no polypeptide there.
rationales: Not all genes in a cell are expressed at any given time. Transcription is the first stage of gene expression, so a gene that is not transcribed in a cell type gives no mRNA and no polypeptide there.
A student who thinks differentiated cells discard genes picks this. The stem states that both cell types contain the gene; the difference is in whether the gene is transcribed.

A student who locates all control at translation picks this. Transcription is the key stage at which a gene is switched on or off; in liver cells the gene is not transcribed, so there is no mRNA to translate.
A student who believes every gene is expressed in every cell picks this. A liver cell does not make the beta chain at all, because the gene is not transcribed in liver cells.

mcqs.q: Why is transcription regarded as a key stage at which the expression of a gene can be switched on or off?
options: Every gene in a cell is transcribed and translated all the time, so expression is not switched on or off at any stage.
It is the first stage of gene expression, so a gene that is not transcribed produces no mRNA and no polypeptide.
All genes in a cell are transcribed at all times, so expression is switched on and off only at translation.
It is the stage at which amino acids are assembled into a chain, so it decides which protein is made.
mcqs.specStatementText: Transcription is where gene expression is switched on or off
mcqs.explain: Transcription is the first stage of gene expression. If a gene is not transcribed there is no mRNA, so nothing further in the expression of that gene can happen; switching transcription on or off switches the gene on or off.
rationales: A student who thinks every gene is always expressed picks this. Not all genes in a cell are expressed at any given time; a gene that is not transcribed produces no mRNA and no polypeptide, so transcription is the stage that is switched on and off.

Transcription is the first stage of gene expression. If a gene is not transcribed there is no mRNA, so nothing further in the expression of that gene can happen; switching transcription on or off switches the gene on or off.

A student who locates the control of expression at translation picks this. Not all genes are transcribed at any given time; because transcription is the first stage, switching it off stops the mRNA being made at all, so it is the key stage at which a gene is switched on or off.
A student who has swapped transcription and translation picks this. Amino acids are assembled in translation; transcription produces the mRNA and is the key control stage because it comes first.

mcqs.q: What happens during translation?
options: A base sequence of DNA is used as a template to make a complementary mRNA molecule inside the cell nucleus.
Ribosomes convert the bases of the mRNA into amino acids, which are then joined into a chain.
The base sequence of an mRNA molecule is used to determine the sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide.
Amino acids are joined into a polypeptide inside the nucleus, right beside the DNA of the gene that codes for it.
mcqs.specStatementText: Translation: a ribosome turns mRNA codons into a polypeptide
mcqs.explain: Translation is the synthesis of a polypeptide from mRNA: the base sequence of the mRNA, read as codons, is translated into the amino acid sequence of the polypeptide on a ribosome.
rationales: A student who has swapped the two terms picks this. Making mRNA on a DNA template is transcription; translation is the synthesis of a polypeptide from the mRNA.
A student who thinks amino acids are made from bases picks this. The amino acids already exist in the cytoplasm and are brought by tRNA; the mRNA only determines the order in which they are joined.
Translation is the synthesis of a polypeptide from mRNA: the base sequence of the mRNA, read as codons, is translated into the amino acid sequence of the polypeptide on a ribosome.
A student who keeps the whole process in the nucleus picks this. Translation takes place on ribosomes in the cytoplasm, after the mRNA has left the nucleus.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the binding of mRNA and tRNA to a ribosome is correct?
options: The mRNA binds to the large subunit, because it is the larger molecule, and the tRNAs bind to the small subunit.
The mRNA binds to the small subunit, and only one tRNA can bind to the large subunit at any moment.
The mRNA binds to the small subunit, and every tRNA needed for the polypeptide binds along it at once.
The mRNA binds to the small subunit, and two tRNAs can bind to the large subunit at the same time.
mcqs.specStatementText: What mRNA, the ribosome and tRNA each do
mcqs.explain: mRNA binds to the small subunit of the ribosome, and two tRNAs can bind simultaneously to the large subunit, allowing a peptide bond to form between the amino acid on one and the polypeptide on the other.
rationales: A student who matches molecule size to subunit size picks this. It is the small subunit that binds the mRNA; the tRNA binding sites are on the large subunit.
A student who pictures one tRNA delivering at a time picks this. Two tRNAs bind simultaneously, so the amino acid on the new tRNA can be joined to the chain held by the other.
A student who takes diagrams of several tRNAs literally picks this. Only two tRNAs are bound at a time, and the ribosome works along the mRNA stepwise.

mRNA binds to the small subunit of the ribosome, and two tRNAs can bind simultaneously to the large subunit, allowing a peptide bond to form between the amino acid on one and the polypeptide on the other.

mcqs.q: A cell contains many different kinds of tRNA molecule. What is the role of a tRNA during translation?
options: It brings a specific amino acid to the ribosome and pairs its anticodon with the matching codon on the mRNA.
It binds to a codon first and then collects from the cytoplasm whichever amino acid that codon specifies.
It delivers an amino acid and remains bonded to it, becoming part of the finished polypeptide chain.
It carries the mRNA bases that the ribosome converts into the amino acids of the polypeptide.
mcqs.specStatementText: What mRNA, the ribosome and tRNA each do
mcqs.explain: Each tRNA carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon complementary to the codons for that amino acid, so complementary base pairing at the ribosome delivers the amino acid the codon specifies.
rationales: Each tRNA carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon complementary to the codons for that amino acid, so complementary base pairing at the ribosome delivers the amino acid the codon specifies.
A student who thinks the codon tells the tRNA what to fetch picks this. The amino acid is attached to the tRNA before it reaches the ribosome; the codon selects which loaded tRNA binds.
A student who thinks tRNAs stay in the chain picks this. Once its amino acid has been joined to the polypeptide by a peptide bond, the tRNA leaves the ribosome and is reused.
A student who thinks amino acids are made from bases picks this. tRNA carries an amino acid, not bases to be converted; the mRNA bases only specify which amino acid is added.

mcqs.q: The start codon on an mRNA molecule is AUG. Which tRNA anticodon binds to this codon, and how is it held there?
options: AUG, the same three bases as the codon
UAC, held to the codon by hydrogen bonds
TAC, with thymine pairing to adenine
UAC, bonded to the codon by covalent bonds
mcqs.specStatementText: Codon and anticodon pair by complementary bases
mcqs.explain: The anticodon is complementary to the codon: A pairs with U, U with A and G with C, giving UAC. The codon and anticodon are held together by hydrogen bonds, which break when the tRNA leaves.
rationales: A student who reads 'matching' as 'identical' picks this. The anticodon pairs with the codon by complementary base pairing, so it is UAC, not AUG.
The anticodon is complementary to the codon: A pairs with U, U with A and G with C, giving UAC. The codon and anticodon are held together by hydrogen bonds, which break when the tRNA leaves.
A student who applies the DNA pairing rules picks this. tRNA is RNA and contains uracil, not thymine, so the base that pairs with the A of the codon is U.

A student who thinks the ribosome bonds the tRNA to the mRNA picks this. Codon and anticodon pair by hydrogen bonds, which must break so the tRNA can leave; covalent bonds form only between amino acids.

mcqs.q: Why does the genetic code use codons of three bases rather than two?
options: Two bases would give 16 codons, which is close enough to 20 for nearly all the amino acids to be coded.
Three bases allow each codon to code for up to three different amino acids whenever these are needed.
Three bases give 64 possible codons, enough for 20 amino acids, whereas two bases give only 16.
Three bases let the ribosome start reading at any point, since any group of three is a codon.
mcqs.specStatementText: Why the code uses triplets, and what degenerate and universal mean
mcqs.explain: With four bases, two-base codons give 4 × 4 = 16 combinations, fewer than the 20 amino acids used in polypeptides. Three-base codons give 4 × 4 × 4 = 64, more than enough, so a triplet code is the shortest that works.
rationales: A student who has not seen the constraint picks this. Sixteen codons cannot specify 20 amino acids; every amino acid needs at least one codon of its own.
A student who thinks the code is ambiguous picks this. Each codon specifies only one amino acid; the number of bases sets how many different codons exist, not how many amino acids one codon can mean.

With four bases, two-base codons give 4 × 4 = 16 combinations, fewer than the 20 amino acids used in polypeptides. Three-base codons give 4 × 4 × 4 = 64, more than enough, so a triplet code is the shortest that works.

A student without a fixed reading frame picks this. Codons are read in a fixed frame from the start codon, and reading from another base gives a wrong sequence; the triplet length is about having enough codons.

mcqs.q: The genetic code is described as degenerate. What does this mean?
options: A single codon can code for two or more different amino acids.
The same codons code for the same amino acids in all organisms.
Some amino acids are coded for by two bases and some by three bases.
Most amino acids are coded for by more than one codon.
mcqs.specStatementText: Why the code uses triplets, and what degenerate and universal mean
mcqs.explain: Degeneracy means that several codons can specify the same amino acid: 61 codons code for 20 amino acids, so for example GGU, GGC, GGA and GGG all code for glycine.
rationales: A student who reverses the many-to-one relationship picks this. The code is degenerate but not ambiguous: a codon always specifies the same single amino acid.
A student who has interchanged the two terms picks this. This is universality; degeneracy is about several codons sharing one amino acid.
A student who takes 'degenerate' to mean irregular picks this. Every codon is exactly three bases long; degeneracy refers to the number of codons per amino acid, not the number of bases per codon.
Degeneracy means that several codons can specify the same amino acid: 61 codons code for 20 amino acids, so for example GGU, GGC, GGA and GGG all code for glycine.

mcqs.q: The gene for human insulin has been inserted into bacteria, which then translate it into a polypeptide with the same amino acid sequence as the polypeptide made in human cells. Which feature of the genetic code makes this possible?
options: Universality: the bacterium's tRNAs assign exactly the same amino acids to the codons as human cells do.
Universality: bacteria and humans have the same genes, so the bacterium already had an insulin gene.
Degeneracy: each codon can be read as several amino acids, so the bacterium can make any protein.
Complementary pairing: bacterial tRNA anticodons pair directly with the bases of the inserted DNA.
mcqs.specStatementText: Why the code uses triplets, and what degenerate and universal mean
mcqs.explain: The genetic code is universal: with minor exceptions, the same codons specify the same amino acids in all organisms, so the bacterium translates the human mRNA into the same amino acid sequence.
rationales: The genetic code is universal: with minor exceptions, the same codons specify the same amino acids in all organisms, so the bacterium translates the human mRNA into the same amino acid sequence.
A student who takes universal to mean 'same genes' picks this. Universality is about the meaning of codons, not the genes; bacteria have no insulin gene, which is why one had to be inserted.

A student who thinks degenerate means ambiguous picks this. Each codon specifies one amino acid; the bacterium makes the human polypeptide because it reads the codons the same way, not because it can read them differently.
A student who thinks tRNA pairs with DNA picks this. The inserted gene is transcribed into mRNA first, and it is the shared meaning of the mRNA codons that makes the product identical.

mcqs.q: Part of an mRNA molecule, written in the order in which it is translated, has the base sequence AUGGGCAACAGA. The genetic code table gives: AUG methionine, GGC glycine, AAC asparagine, AGA arginine, UAC tyrosine, CCG proline, UUG leucine, UCU serine, UGG tryptophan, GCA alanine, ACA threonine. Which amino acid is the third in the polypeptide?
options: arginine
asparagine
leucine
threonine
mcqs.specStatementText: Reading an mRNA sequence with the codon table
mcqs.explain: Reading from the start codon in groups of three gives AUG GGC AAC AGA: methionine, glycine, asparagine, arginine. The third codon, AAC, codes for asparagine.
rationales: A student who treats AUG as a start signal only, and begins counting from GGC, makes arginine (AGA) the third amino acid. AUG codes for methionine, which is the first amino acid, so the third is asparagine.
Reading from the start codon in groups of three gives AUG GGC AAC AGA: methionine, glycine, asparagine, arginine. The third codon, AAC, codes for asparagine.

A student who first writes the complementary sequence (UAC CCG UUG UCU) and looks that up picks leucine. The table is for mRNA codons and the sequence given is already mRNA, so no complement should be taken.
A student who begins reading from the second base (UGG GCA ACA) picks threonine. The reading frame is fixed by the start codon AUG, so codons must be counted from the first base.

mcqs.q: An mRNA molecule has the base sequence AUGUUUGCUUAAGGC, read from the first base. The genetic code table gives: AUG methionine (start), UUU phenylalanine, GCU alanine, UAA stop, GGC glycine. How many amino acids are in the polypeptide translated from it?
options: two amino acids
four amino acids
three amino acids
fifteen amino acids
mcqs.specStatementText: Reading an mRNA sequence with the codon table
mcqs.explain: The codons are AUG UUU GCU UAA GGC. AUG gives methionine, UUU phenylalanine and GCU alanine; UAA is a stop codon, so translation ends there and GGC is never translated. The polypeptide has three amino acids.
rationales: A student who does not count the start codon picks this. AUG codes for methionine as well as marking the start, so methionine, phenylalanine and alanine make three.
A student who reads past the stop codon to include GGC picks this. UAA ends translation, so the glycine codon after it is not translated.

The codons are AUG UUU GCU UAA GGC. AUG gives methionine, UUU phenylalanine and GCU alanine; UAA is a stop codon, so translation ends there and GGC is never translated. The polypeptide has three amino acids.
A student who thinks each base codes for one amino acid picks this. The code is a triplet code, so 15 bases form 5 codons, of which one is a stop codon and only three are translated.

mcqs.q: How is the polypeptide chain lengthened during translation?
options: All the tRNAs first line up along the whole length of the mRNA, and their amino acids are then joined together in one step.
Each tRNA stays attached to its own amino acid, so the chain is a series of tRNAs joined through their amino acids.
Each new amino acid is held to the previous one by hydrogen bonds, like those between codon and anticodon.
The ribosome moves along the mRNA one codon at a time, and a peptide bond links each new amino acid to the chain.
mcqs.specStatementText: Elongation: one codon, one peptide bond, one step along
mcqs.explain: Elongation is stepwise: the ribosome moves along the mRNA one codon at a time, a tRNA pairs with each codon in turn, and the amino acid it carries is linked to the growing polypeptide by a peptide bond.
rationales: A student who takes a diagram of many tRNAs literally picks this. Only two tRNAs are on the ribosome at once, and amino acids are added one at a time as the ribosome moves.
A student who leaves the tRNAs in the chain picks this. Each tRNA is released once its amino acid has been joined by a peptide bond, and the chain consists of amino acids only.
A student who generalizes hydrogen bonding to the whole topic picks this. Amino acids are linked by peptide bonds, which are covalent; hydrogen bonds hold codon to anticodon only temporarily.

Elongation is stepwise: the ribosome moves along the mRNA one codon at a time, a tRNA pairs with each codon in turn, and the amino acid it carries is linked to the growing polypeptide by a peptide bond.

mcqs.q: An antibiotic stops the ribosome from moving along the mRNA but does not affect the binding of tRNAs or the formation of peptide bonds. What effect will this have on translation of an mRNA?
options: Only the first peptide bond forms, since the next codon cannot be moved into place for a tRNA to bind.
Translation is unaffected, because all the tRNAs bind along the mRNA before any peptide bonds are formed.
Translation is unaffected, because each tRNA leaves the ribosome before the next one binds to the mRNA.
The chain still grows, because each tRNA stays attached to its amino acid and the next tRNA simply joins onto it.
mcqs.specStatementText: Elongation: one codon, one peptide bond, one step along
mcqs.explain: Two tRNAs can bind and a peptide bond can form between their amino acids, but the chain then grows only if the ribosome moves one codon along so that the used tRNA leaves and the next codon is exposed. Without movement, elongation stops.
rationales: Two tRNAs can bind and a peptide bond can form between their amino acids, but the chain then grows only if the ribosome moves one codon along so that the used tRNA leaves and the next codon is exposed. Without movement, elongation stops.
A student who pictures all the tRNAs lining up at once picks this. Only two tRNAs are bound at a time, so each further codon has to be brought into the ribosome by stepwise movement.
A student who thinks one tRNA is bound at a time picks this. Even so, the next codon must be moved into the ribosome for the next tRNA to pair with it, and the ribosome cannot move.
A student who thinks tRNAs chain together picks this. tRNAs leave after giving up their amino acid, and new tRNAs bind to codons in the ribosome, which the ribosome must move along the mRNA to reach.

mcqs.q: In the allele that causes sickle cell anaemia, the sixth codon of the mRNA for the beta chain of haemoglobin is GUG instead of GAG. GAG codes for glutamic acid and GUG codes for valine. What is the effect of this mutation on the protein?
options: One amino acid out of more than a hundred is changed, too small a difference to alter the structure or function of haemoglobin.
Valine replaces glutamic acid at one position, which alters haemoglobin enough for it to form fibres at low oxygen concentrations.
The reading frame is shifted from the sixth codon onward, so every amino acid after it in the beta chain is different.
The codon GUG is degenerate, so the ribosome can still insert glutamic acid and the haemoglobin produced is normal.
mcqs.specStatementText: A single base change can change a protein
mcqs.explain: This base substitution changes one codon and so one amino acid. The valine on the surface of the beta chain makes deoxygenated haemoglobin molecules stick together into fibres, which distort the red blood cells into a sickle shape.
rationales: A student reasoning proportionally picks this. A protein's function depends on its exact sequence; this single substitution is enough to cause a serious disease.

This base substitution changes one codon and so one amino acid. The valine on the surface of the beta chain makes deoxygenated haemoglobin molecules stick together into fibres, which distort the red blood cells into a sickle shape.
A student who attaches the frameshift effect to every point mutation picks this. A substitution leaves the number of bases unchanged, so only the sixth codon is altered.

A student who thinks a codon can be read as more than one amino acid picks this. GUG always codes for valine; degeneracy means several codons for one amino acid, not several amino acids for one codon.

mcqs.q: A base substitution in a gene changes an mRNA codon from GGU to GGC. Both codons code for glycine. What is the effect on the polypeptide?
options: Its structure changes, because a different codon is bound to give a different amino acid.
Every amino acid after this point changes, because the reading frame has been shifted.
There is no effect, because the same amino acid, glycine, is inserted at that position.
Glycine may be replaced, because GGC can also code for a different amino acid.
mcqs.specStatementText: A single base change can change a protein
mcqs.explain: Because the genetic code is degenerate, GGU and GGC both code for glycine. The polypeptide's amino acid sequence, and so its structure, is unchanged by this silent substitution.
rationales: A student who expects every substitution to change the protein picks this. Degeneracy means a changed codon can still specify the same amino acid, as here.
A student who thinks all point mutations shift the frame picks this. A substitution replaces one base with another and leaves the reading frame intact.
Because the genetic code is degenerate, GGU and GGC both code for glycine. The polypeptide's amino acid sequence, and so its structure, is unchanged by this silent substitution.
A student who thinks the code is ambiguous picks this. Each codon specifies one amino acid only; GGC always codes for glycine.

mcqs.q: Two mutations occur near the start of the coding sequence of the same gene, in different cells: in one cell a single base is substituted; in the other a single base is inserted. Which mutation is more likely to change the structure of the protein, and why?
options: Neither is likely to, because each changes only a single base and so can affect at most one amino acid.
The substitution, because a substitution is certain to change an amino acid, while an insertion adds only one.
Neither is likely to, because the ribosome recognizes each codon wherever it starts reading.
The insertion, because it shifts the reading frame so that every codon after it is read differently.
mcqs.specStatementText: A single base change can change a protein
mcqs.explain: Adding one base changes how all the following bases are grouped into codons, so the amino acid sequence from that point onward is altered. A substitution changes at most one amino acid and may be silent.
rationales: A student who assumes a one-base change means a one-amino-acid change picks this. An insertion shifts the reading frame and alters every subsequent codon.
A student who thinks every substitution changes an amino acid picks this. Many substitutions are silent, and an insertion does not add one amino acid but changes the reading of all that follow.
A student without a fixed reading frame picks this. The ribosome reads consecutive triplets from the start codon, so an inserted base makes it read every later triplet in the wrong frame.

Adding one base changes how all the following bases are grouped into codons, so the amino acid sequence from that point onward is altered. A substitution changes at most one amino acid and may be silent.

mcqs.q: During transcription, RNA polymerase adds each new nucleotide to the free 3' end of the growing RNA strand. What does this mean for the direction of transcription?
options: The RNA is synthesized 5' to 3' while the template strand is read 3' to 5'.
The RNA is synthesized 5' to 3' and the template strand is read in the same 5' to 3' direction.
The RNA is synthesized 3' to 5', because the 3' end is where the chain is being extended.
The RNA can be synthesized in either direction, since nucleotides can be joined at either end.
mcqs.specStatementText: Both transcription and translation run 5' to 3'
mcqs.explain: Adding nucleotides to the 3' end means the RNA grows from its 5' end towards its 3' end, which is what 5' to 3' transcription means. The strands are antiparallel, so the template is read from its 3' end towards its 5' end.
rationales: Adding nucleotides to the 3' end means the RNA grows from its 5' end towards its 3' end, which is what 5' to 3' transcription means. The strands are antiparallel, so the template is read from its 3' end towards its 5' end.
A student who forgets that the strands are antiparallel picks this. The RNA runs opposite to the template it pairs with, so the template is read 3' to 5'.
A student who names the direction by the end being extended picks this. Direction of synthesis is from the first nucleotide (5' end) to the last, so extending the 3' end is 5' to 3' synthesis.
A student who gives strands no direction picks this. RNA polymerase can add only to the 3' hydroxyl, so synthesis is always 5' to 3'.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the direction of translation is correct?
options: The ribosome can begin at either end of the mRNA, since the start codon is recognized wherever it is met.
The ribosome moves along the mRNA from its 5' end towards its 3' end, so the codon nearest the 5' end is translated first.
The ribosome moves along the mRNA from its 3' end towards its 5' end, matching the direction the template is read.
The ribosome begins at the 5' cap and translates every base up to and including the poly-A tail at the 3' end.
mcqs.specStatementText: Both transcription and translation run 5' to 3'
mcqs.explain: Translation is 5' to 3': the small subunit binds near the 5' end of the mRNA, finds the start codon and the ribosome moves towards the 3' end, so the polypeptide is built from the 5'-most codon onward.
rationales: A student who gives the mRNA no direction picks this. The ribosome binds at the 5' end and moves towards the 3' end; it does not begin from the 3' end.

Translation is 5' to 3': the small subunit binds near the 5' end of the mRNA, finds the start codon and the ribosome moves towards the 3' end, so the polypeptide is built from the 5'-most codon onward.
A student who transfers the 3' to 5' reading of the DNA template to the mRNA picks this. The mRNA is read in its own 5' to 3' direction, the same direction in which it was synthesized.
A student who treats the whole mRNA as code picks this. Translation runs 5' to 3' but only from the start codon to the stop codon; the cap and tail are not translated.

mcqs.q: A gene is transcribed in muscle cells but not in skin cells, although the DNA of the two cell types is identical. Which statement explains this in terms of initiation of transcription at the promoter?
options: RNA polymerase binds to the promoter by itself in both cell types, so the difference between the two cell types must arise at a stage after transcription.
In muscle cells the promoter is transcribed as the first part of the mRNA, and this acts as a signal for the gene to be expressed.
Muscle cells contain transcription factors that bind to the promoter, allowing RNA polymerase to bind and begin transcription; skin cells lack them.
All genes are transcribed in every cell, and the mRNA for this gene is simply broken down faster in skin cells than in muscle cells.
mcqs.specStatementText: Transcription starts at the promoter, once transcription factors bind
mcqs.explain: In eukaryotes, transcription is initiated when transcription factors bind to the promoter and enable RNA polymerase to bind. Cell types differ in the transcription factors they contain, so the same gene is switched on in one and off in another.
rationales: A student who thinks RNA polymerase needs no help picks this. Eukaryotic RNA polymerase cannot initiate without transcription factors at the promoter, and the stem states that the gene is not transcribed in skin cells.
A student who thinks the promoter is copied into the mRNA picks this. The promoter is the DNA sequence where the transcription machinery binds; transcription begins after it.

In eukaryotes, transcription is initiated when transcription factors bind to the promoter and enable RNA polymerase to bind. Cell types differ in the transcription factors they contain, so the same gene is switched on in one and off in another.
A student who thinks every gene is always transcribed picks this. Not all genes are transcribed in every cell, and here the stem states that skin cells do not transcribe the gene at all.

mcqs.q: Which statement about non-coding sequences in eukaryotic DNA is correct?
options: Non-coding sequences such as introns and telomeres have no function at all and so are never transcribed into RNA.
Every gene codes for a polypeptide, so tRNA and rRNA are both produced by translation of their own mRNA molecules.
The promoter of a gene is transcribed and forms the first codons of the mRNA for that gene.
The genes for tRNA and rRNA are transcribed, but their RNA products are never translated into polypeptides.
mcqs.specStatementText: Most eukaryotic DNA does not code for polypeptides, but has functions
mcqs.explain: Genes for tRNAs and rRNAs are non-coding in the sense that their products are functional RNA molecules, not polypeptides: they are transcribed but never translated. Introns are also transcribed but are removed before translation, while promoters and telomeres are neither translated nor part of any mRNA.
rationales: A student who equates non-coding with junk picks this. Telomeres protect chromosome ends, promoters regulate expression, and introns are transcribed before being spliced out.
A student who defines a gene by its protein product picks this. tRNA and rRNA are made directly by transcription of their genes and are never translated.
A student who confuses the promoter with the start of the mRNA picks this. The promoter is where RNA polymerase binds; it is a regulator of expression, not part of the coding sequence.

Genes for tRNAs and rRNAs are non-coding in the sense that their products are functional RNA molecules, not polypeptides: they are transcribed but never translated. Introns are also transcribed but are removed before translation, while promoters and telomeres are neither translated nor part of any mRNA.

mcqs.q: A eukaryotic gene contains three exons separated by two introns. Which statement describes the mature mRNA produced from this gene?
options: It contains the three exons joined together, with a 5' cap and a 3' poly-A tail added on.
It contains the three exons only, because the introns were cut out of the DNA before the gene was transcribed.
It contains the two introns joined together, because the exons were the sections removed by splicing.
It contains all five sections, with the cap and tail translated as extra amino acids at each end.
mcqs.specStatementText: Pre-mRNA is spliced and capped before it leaves the nucleus
mcqs.explain: Post-transcriptional modification removes the introns from the pre-mRNA and splices the exons together, and adds a 5' cap and a 3' poly-A tail that stabilize the transcript. The result is the mature mRNA.
rationales: Post-transcriptional modification removes the introns from the pre-mRNA and splices the exons together, and adds a 5' cap and a 3' poly-A tail that stabilize the transcript. The result is the mature mRNA.
A student who removes introns from the gene picks this. The whole gene, introns included, is transcribed into pre-mRNA; the introns are removed from the RNA, and the DNA is unchanged.
A student who has the names the wrong way round picks this. Exons are expressed and retained; introns are the intervening sequences that are removed.
A student who treats everything on the mRNA as code picks this. The introns are removed, and the cap and tail are not translated; they stabilize the mRNA.

mcqs.q: What is the role of the 5' cap and the 3' poly-A tail added to a eukaryotic mRNA transcript?
options: They are translated, adding a short run of extra amino acids to each end of the polypeptide.
They stabilize the mRNA, protecting it from being broken down before it is translated.
They mark the positions of the introns so that the splicing enzymes know which sections to remove.
They have no function, being left over from transcription of non-coding DNA at each end of the gene.
mcqs.specStatementText: Pre-mRNA is spliced and capped before it leaves the nucleus
mcqs.explain: The 5' cap and 3' poly-A tail are added after transcription to stabilize mRNA transcripts, so that the mRNA survives to be exported from the nucleus and translated.
rationales: A student who assumes every part of the mRNA is code picks this. Translation runs from the start codon to the stop codon; the cap and tail lie outside this and add no amino acids.
The 5' cap and 3' poly-A tail are added after transcription to stabilize mRNA transcripts, so that the mRNA survives to be exported from the nucleus and translated.
A student who muddles the modifications picks this. The cap and tail are at the two ends of the transcript; introns are internal and are recognized by their own sequences.
A student who equates non-coding with functionless picks this. The cap and tail are not transcribed from the gene at all; they are added afterwards and have the function of stabilizing the mRNA.

mcqs.q: The human genome contains about 20 000 protein-coding genes, yet human cells produce well over 20 000 different polypeptides. Which process accounts for this?
options: Mutation of the gene during transcription, so that each transcript carries a slightly different base sequence.
Degeneracy of the genetic code, which allows a codon to be translated as different amino acids in different cells.
Alternative splicing, in which different combinations of exons from one pre-mRNA are joined to give different mature mRNAs.
Duplication of each gene during differentiation, so that every different polypeptide is coded for by a separate gene of its own.
mcqs.specStatementText: One gene can give several polypeptides by splicing exons differently
mcqs.explain: Splicing together different combinations of exons allows a single gene to code for several different polypeptides, so the number of polypeptides an organism makes can far exceed its number of genes.
rationales: A student who treats mutation as a routine copying error picks this. Transcription copies the gene faithfully; the variants arise from combining exons differently, not from changing the sequence.
A student who thinks the code is ambiguous picks this. Each codon specifies one amino acid in every cell; degeneracy means several codons per amino acid, which cannot create new polypeptides.
Splicing together different combinations of exons allows a single gene to code for several different polypeptides, so the number of polypeptides an organism makes can far exceed its number of genes.
A student holding 'one gene, one polypeptide' picks this. Somatic cells all have the same genes; one gene gives several polypeptides through alternative splicing.

mcqs.q: Which sequence of events initiates translation of an mRNA in a eukaryotic cell?
options: The complete ribosome binds directly to the start codon as a single unit, and the initiator tRNA then enters the ribosome and pairs with the codon.
The small subunit binds to the 3' end of the mRNA and moves along until it reaches the start codon, where the large subunit attaches.
The small subunit binds at the start codon, and the initiator tRNA enters at the E site before the large subunit attaches to it.
The small subunit binds to the 5' end of the mRNA and moves to the start codon; the initiator tRNA binds there; then the large subunit attaches.
mcqs.specStatementText: How translation starts, and the A, P and E sites
mcqs.explain: Initiation begins with attachment of the small ribosomal subunit to the 5' terminal of the mRNA. It moves to the start codon, the initiator tRNA carrying methionine pairs with AUG, and the large subunit then attaches so that a second tRNA can enter the A site.
rationales: A student who pictures the ribosome as a single unit picks this. The small subunit binds first, at the 5' end, and the large subunit attaches only after the initiator tRNA is in place at the start codon.
A student who gives the mRNA no direction picks this. The small subunit attaches to the 5' terminal of the mRNA and moves towards the 3' end to find the start codon.
A student who reads E as 'entry' picks this. The initiator tRNA occupies the P site once the large subunit has attached; the E site is the exit site from which used tRNAs leave.

Initiation begins with attachment of the small ribosomal subunit to the 5' terminal of the mRNA. It moves to the start codon, the initiator tRNA carrying methionine pairs with AUG, and the large subunit then attaches so that a second tRNA can enter the A site.

mcqs.q: During elongation, what are the roles of the A, P and E sites of the ribosome?
options: A tRNA carrying the next amino acid enters the A site, the tRNA holding the growing polypeptide is in the P site, and a used tRNA leaves from the E site.
A tRNA enters the ribosome at the E site, moves to the P site where its amino acid is added to the growing chain, and finally leaves the ribosome from the A site.
Only one site is occupied at any one time: a tRNA enters the A site, passes through the P site and then the E site, and leaves before the next tRNA enters.
The tRNAs in all three sites remain attached to their amino acids, so the polypeptide is held to the ribosome by three tRNAs at once.
mcqs.specStatementText: How translation starts, and the A, P and E sites
mcqs.explain: The A site accepts the incoming tRNA whose anticodon pairs with the codon, the P site holds the tRNA attached to the polypeptide, and after the ribosome moves one codon the tRNA that has given up the chain sits in the E site and exits.
rationales: The A site accepts the incoming tRNA whose anticodon pairs with the codon, the P site holds the tRNA attached to the polypeptide, and after the ribosome moves one codon the tRNA that has given up the chain sits in the E site and exits.
A student who reads E as 'entry' picks this. Entry is at the A site, and the E (exit) site is where a tRNA that has given up its amino acid sits before leaving.
A student who thinks one tRNA is bound at a time picks this. Two tRNAs are bound during peptide bond formation, one in the A site and one in the P site.

A student who thinks tRNAs stay bonded to their amino acids picks this. Only the tRNA in the P site (or, just after a peptide bond forms, the A site) holds the polypeptide; the E-site tRNA has no amino acid.

mcqs.q: Insulin consists of two polypeptide chains, A and B, held together by disulfide bonds, yet it is coded for by a single gene. How is functional insulin produced?
options: Two separate polypeptides, A and B, are translated from the gene and are then joined to each other by disulfide bonds in the Golgi apparatus.
Pre-proinsulin loses its signal sequence to give proinsulin; a central section is then cut out, leaving the two chains.
The polypeptide made by translation is already insulin, and the two chains form as it folds when it leaves the ribosome.
Alternative splicing of the insulin pre-mRNA produces two different mature mRNAs, one of which codes for each of the two chains.
mcqs.specStatementText: Many polypeptides are cut or altered before they work
mcqs.explain: This is the two-stage modification of pre-proinsulin: removal of the signal sequence gives proinsulin, which folds and forms disulfide bonds, and removal of the central section then leaves the A and B chains joined as active insulin.
rationales: A student who explains two chains by two polypeptides picks this. One polypeptide is translated; the two chains are what remains of it after a central section is removed.

This is the two-stage modification of pre-proinsulin: removal of the signal sequence gives proinsulin, which folds and forms disulfide bonds, and removal of the central section then leaves the A and B chains joined as active insulin.
A student who thinks translation makes the finished protein picks this. Pre-proinsulin is not functional; two sections must be removed before it becomes insulin.
A student who over-applies alternative splicing picks this. The two chains of insulin are not splice variants; they are two parts of a single polypeptide cut after translation.

mcqs.q: Why does a cell continually break down some of its proteins in proteasomes while synthesizing new ones?
options: Proteins are permanent once they have been made, so proteasomes act only when a cell has been badly damaged or is about to die.
Proteasomes break down proteins only when the cell is short of glucose and needs amino acids as a source of energy.
Sustaining a functional proteome needs constant turnover: proteins no longer needed are removed and their amino acids reused.
The amino acids released by proteasomes are waste products that the cell must excrete, so breakdown removes unwanted material.
mcqs.specStatementText: Proteins are constantly broken down and rebuilt
mcqs.explain: The proteome changes as the cell's needs change. Proteasomes break down proteins that are damaged or no longer required, and the amino acids released are reused in the synthesis of the proteins the cell now needs.
rationales: A student who sees proteins as permanent parts picks this. Protein breakdown by proteasomes is continuous in healthy cells and is needed to keep the proteome functional.
A student who knows protein breakdown only from starvation picks this. Proteasome activity is a normal, constant part of regulating which proteins are present, whatever the energy supply.

The proteome changes as the cell's needs change. Proteasomes break down proteins that are damaged or no longer required, and the amino acids released are reused in the synthesis of the proteins the cell now needs.
A student who applies the GCSE idea of excreting excess amino acids picks this. The amino acids from proteasomes are recycled into new proteins; the point of breakdown is turnover, not excretion.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025); topic D1.2 Protein synthesis

Base pairing sets the RNA sequence; hydrogen bonds let it go
A DNA template can be read again and again without changing
Transcription is where gene expression is switched on or off
Translation: a ribosome turns mRNA codons into a polypeptide
What mRNA, the ribosome and tRNA each do
Codon and anticodon pair by complementary bases
Why the code uses triplets, and what degenerate and universal mean
Reading an mRNA sequence with the codon table
Elongation: one codon, one peptide bond, one step along

Transcription starts at the promoter, once transcription factors bind

Pre-mRNA is spliced and capped before it leaves the nucleus

scopeNotes.howHonoured: The SL objects on D1.2.4 test only that different cells transcribe different genes and that a gene that is not transcribed is not expressed. No mechanism of regulation (transcription factors, operons, DNA methylation, chromatin changes, non-coding RNA) appears in any SL object; transcription factors binding to the promoter appear only in HL objects anchored to D1.2.13.

The objects on D1.2.10 deal only with elongation: the stepwise movement of the ribosome one codon at a time and the formation of peptide bonds to the growing chain. Initiation is treated only in the HL objects on D1.2.17. Termination is not described beyond the fact, needed for D1.2.9, that a stop codon ends the polypeptide; release factors and the disassembly of the ribosome are not mentioned.

Transcription factors are described only as proteins that bind to the promoter and allow RNA polymerase to bind. No transcription factor is named (no TATA-binding protein, no TFII factors) and no structural detail of the promoter (such as the TATA box) is given.

The only examples of non-coding DNA used are the four the guidance lists: sequences that regulate gene expression (promoters and enhancers), introns, telomeres and the genes for rRNA and tRNA. Centromeres, transposons, pseudogenes, satellite DNA and genes for other non-coding RNAs are not mentioned.

Alternative splicing is tested only as the principle that different combinations of exons from one pre-mRNA give different mature mRNAs and so different polypeptides from a single gene. No named gene or protein with splice variants is used; the human genome gene count is used only as a context for why the principle matters.

Proteasomes are treated only as the site where proteins that are no longer needed or are damaged are broken down to amino acids that are recycled into new proteins. The tagging of proteins with ubiquitin, the structure of the proteasome and lysosomal or autophagic breakdown are not mentioned.

omitted.sequence: no authored ordering; would require inventing a sequence
